results.question: What is the half-life of carbon-14 used in radiocarbon dating?
points: 说明它用于放射性碳定年

searxng.finalText:
The half-life of carbon-14 (¹⁴C) used in radiocarbon dating is **5,730 years** [1][3][7]. Some sources cite the value as 5,700 ± 30 years [5]. This means that after 5,730 years, half of the carbon-14 in a sample has decayed [3], which underpins the method's ability to date organic materials [2].

Sources:
- [Radiocarbon Dating | Museum of Anthropology](https://anthromuseum.missouri.edu/radiocarbon-dating)
- [¹⁴C decays — NOAA GML](https://gml.noaa.gov/education/isotopes/decay.html)
- [Carbon-14 dating technique — CIRAM](https://www.ciram-lab.com/en/our-techniques/dating-techniques/carbon-14-and-radiocarbon/)
- [The Half-Life of ¹⁴C — Radiocarbon](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/radiocarbon/article/halflife-of-14cwhy-is-it-so-long/40C969D635697E923338763B56402862)

official.finalText:
The half-life of carbon-14 is approximately **5,730 years** — the "Libby half-life" conventionally used to calculate radiocarbon ages. More precise modern measurements place it at about **5,700 years** (5,700 ± 30 years) [1][3][8].

- [Radiocarbon Dating (Schwarcz)](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9781315663999-12/radiocarbon-dating-schwarcz) [1]
- [Nature Reviews Methods Primers: Radiocarbon dating](https://experiments.springernature.com/nature/primers/10.1038/s43586-021-00058-7#1) [3]
- [Principle of ¹⁴C dating (ÚJF CAS)](https://www.ujf.cas.cz/en/our-services/Radiocarbon_laboratory/Principle_of_14C_dating/) [8]

scores.notes: Both correctly state ~5730 years and mention radiocarbon dating; A is slightly better with precise modern value and stronger, directly relevant citations.
